newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Amid protest, Albania president admits mistakes.
newsitem.headline: Amid protest, Albania president admits mistakes.

text.p: Albanian police stepped aside on Saturday and let thousands of cheated investors march to demand that the government reimburse millions of dollars in losses and then quit.

"Down with the government", "Police are with us", chanted about 1,000 people in Fier, 110 km (70 miles) south of Tirana. Several thousand people marched through the port town of Vlore, further south, for an 11th day.

In Tirana, President Sali Berisha admitted mistakes in his handling of the pyramid scandal but said responsibility also lay with those who put millions of dollars into high-interest schemes -- and lost everything.

Addressing a meeting of selected supporters, he said the state would not reimburse hundreds of thousands of Albanians who lost their savings and often sold valuables or property to invest in the schemes.
"We will not take this debt on our shoulders. No democratic government would do this. It would be cheating, printing money to pay and creating hyperinflation," he said.
Berisha said another mistake was using riot police to quell unrest in Vlore this week. Three people died during the clashes and scores were injured.
"People should be allowed to demonstrate freely," he said. Demonstrations are virtually banned in Tirana and protests for the past few weeks have been confined to the countryside.
In Fier on Saturday riot police could be seen as protesters marched, chanting and waving to television cameras.
A police commander who declined to be named said: "There is no problem. We have withdrawn the riot police. Let them demonstrate. It's their right."
In Vlore, about 4,000 people marched, carrying the picture of Maliq Banushi, 51, who died of a heart attack during protests this week. "Police killed him" was written below his photograph.
One demonstrator was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks in Vlore.

Traffic police accompanied the crowd in Vlore. Police fled the town after the clashes and returned a few days later. Police commanders said traffic police are back on duty and about 80 percent of the regular police force is working again.

Demonstrators had stoned, stripped and then expelled the Vlore police during Monday's violence, plunging the 90,000 residents of Albania's second port into lawlessness, crime and smuggling of would-be-refugees to Italy.
Many people in the town have been financially ruined since Vlore's local Gjallica scheme collapsed, and they accuse the right-wing government of letting the schemes flourish over the past five years.
Officials in Tirana said prosecutors have now issued international arrest warrants for the failed Gjallica scheme's president Shemsie Kadria and her husband, Gani.

Reports vary widely on how much money was lost by the five companies which have gone bust. News reports in Tirana said Kadria and her husband fled to Turkey and owed creditors $363 million. Other reporters have put the figure at $500 million.
Gjallica's businesses and the personal assets of managers have been seized. The government has ordered banks to freeze deposits of Gjallica managers.
A Tirana appeals court upheld jail sentences of up to three years for three managers of the Arkond firm and ordered them each to pay $150,000 to investors in the scheme which collapsed last year.
